raw_text: Alchivemycin A belongs to a unique class of polyketide natural products isolated from plant-derived actinomycete Streptomyces. It shows potent antibacterial activity and anti-tumour activity. However, its inherent structural complexity and high oxidation state, especially the 2H-tetrahydro-4,6-dioxo-1,2-oxazine (TDO) ring system, present synthetic challenges. Here we report the total synthesis of alchivemycin A using a chemoenzymatic approach that combines de novo skeleton construction and late-stage enzymatic oxidation reactions. The convergen synthesis of the highly functionalized unnatural tetramic acid-bearing intermediate is achieved by boron-alkyl Suzuki−Miyaura cross-coupling, macrolactamization and Lacey–Dieckmann condensation reactions. Eficient enzymatic epoxidations using the redox enzymes AvmO3 and AvmO2 allow rapid access to the desired diepoxide product regio- and stereoselectively. Subsequently, a flavin adenine dinucleotide-dependent enzyme AvmO1 variant optimized via rational protein engineering, AvmO1-Y282R, was used to convert the tetramic acid ring into the TDO ring through a Baeyer–Villiger-type transformation, completing the chemoenzymatic synthesis of alchivemycin A. This work paves the way to further explore the biological functions of alchivemycin A and highlights the utility of chemoenzymatic strategies to tackle synthetic challenges in complex molecule synthesis.

raw_text: It is commonly believed that developing a new generation of antibiotics with a novel mode of action is an effective way to overcome the increasing global threat of antimicrobial resistance<sup>1,2</sup>. In 2010, Igarashi and colleagues isolated a novel polycyclic polyketide natural product, alchivemycin A (1), from the cultural extract of plant-derived actinomycete Streptomyces sp. TP-A0867 (Fig. 1a)<sup>3</sup>. Alchivemycin A (1) shows excellent antibacterial and anti-tumour activity, for example, it exhibited selective antimicrobial activity against Micrococcus luteus with an minimum inhibitory concentration of 32 ng ml<sup>−1</sup> (ref. 3). Remarkably, it also inhibited the invasion of murine colon carcinoma 26-L5 cells into Matrigel with an half-maximal inhibitory concentration of 340 nM without showing any cytotoxic effects<sup>3</sup>. The structure of alchivemycin A (1) was determined by X-ray crystallography and spectroscopic analysis, including <sup>1</sup>H NMR anisotropy experiments on the 2-methoxy-2-phenylacetic acid ester derivative<sup>3</sup>. raw_text: Our group has a long-standing research interest in functionoriented natural product synthesis and subsequent chemical biology studies<sup>4</sup>. Accordingly, we have extensively investigated the total synthe sis of alchivemycin A (1) to facilitate subsequent biological evaluations. The structural complexity of alchivemycin A (1) displays enormous synthetic challenges (Fig. 1b). Several synthetic studies towards alchivemycin A (1) have previously been reported by our group, including the syntheses of the cis-decalin fragment<sup>5,6</sup>, the TDO ring system<sup>7</sup> and the polyhydroxy side-chain fragment<sup>8</sup>. We have also attempted to complete the total synthesis of alchivemycin A (1) by convergent fragment coupling and a Reformatsky-type macrocyclization. However, despite numerous attempts using different conditions and synthetic sequences, the highly functionalized macrocyclic skeleton containing the TDO ring has yet to be established (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 1). Therefore a novel approach needs to be developed to overcome the inherent synthetic challenges in handling labile functional groups and achieving high regio-, chemo- or stereoselectivities with limited chemical transformations at a late stage.

raw_text: The lessons learned from natural product biosynthesis may inspire synthetic chemists to develop new strategies to tackle the challenges of complex natural product synthesis<sup>9–12</sup>. In 2021, Ge and colleagues reported the characterization of six redox enzymes (AvmO1, AvmO2, AvmO3, AvmO4, AvmP and AvmR) in the late-stage metabolic network that leads to the formation of alchivemycin ${ \bf A } ( { \bf 1 } ) ^ { 1 3 }$ These six redox enzymes include three flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)-dependent monooxygenases (AvmO1, AvmO2 and AvmO3), a non-haem α-ketoglutarate $/ \mathsf { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent dioxygenase (AvmO4), a P450 monooxygenase (AvmP) and an $\mathrm { F } _ { 4 2 0 } \cdot$ -dependent oxidoreductase (AvmR). In the biosynthetic pathway (Fig. 1d), starting from compound 2, AvmR reduces the carbonyl group at C-25 to generate compound 3. Subsequently, AvmO3 introduces an epoxy group at C-11 and C-12 to furnish compound 4. Another epoxy group at C-14 and C-15 is established by AvmO2 to generate compound 5. Next, the hydroxy group at C-24 is introduced by AvmP, furnishing compound 6, which is then transformed into TDO-containing compound 7 by AvmO1. The final natural product, alchivemycin A (1), is afforded through oxidation at C-22 by AvmO4. The one-pot enzymatic synthesis of alchivemycin A (1) from compound 2 on a liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) scale was reported by Ge and colleagues (Fig. 1d)<sup>13</sup>. Further biosynthetic investigations by Ge and colleagues revealed that the macrocycle of alchivemycin A (1) can be established via a tandem dehydration–Michael-type addition reaction catalysed by AvmM (ref. 14). Notably, the complete biosynthetic pathway is still to be fully elucidated.

raw_text: Inspired by this biosynthetic discovery<sup>13–16</sup>, we report here the total synthesis of alchivemycin A (1) using a chemoenzymatic approach that combines de novo skeleton construction and late-stage enzymatic oxidation reactions. The convergent synthesis of the highly functionalized unnatural tetramic acid-bearing intermediate was mainly achieved by boron-alkyl Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling, macrolactamization and Lacey–Dieckmann condensation reactions. An enzymatic cascade reaction using two enzymes, AvmO3 and AvmO2, allowed rapid access to the desired diepoxide product regio- and stereoselectively. Subsequently, AvmO1 was used to convert the tetramic acid ring into the TDO ring, resulting in the chemoenzymatic total synthesis of alchivemycin A (1).

Results and discussion

raw_text: Retrosynthetic analysis based on a chemoenzymatic approach Conceivably, the most challenging step in the total synthesis of alchivemycin A (1) is the construction of the TDO ring system at a late stage of the synthesis. Although we have previously developed a synthetic methodology for the formation of the TDO ring<sup>7</sup>, it has proven challenging to implement it in the late-stage synthesis of complex and highly functionalized substrates because of the harsh conditions required. Meanwhile, the chemoenzymatic synthesis of complex natural products has developed rapidly<sup>9–12,17–36</sup>. Therefore, in light of the study of Ge and colleagues described above<sup>13</sup>, we considered that enzymatic catalysis with AvmO1 would represent a promising alternative in the biosynthesis of alchivemycin A (1). Thus, we planned to develop a chemoenzymatic total synthesis of alchivemycin A (1) using AvmO1 to create the TDO ring system from substrates bearing tetramic acid. In addition, we also envisioned that the use of AvmO2 and AvmO3 would enable us to install the two epoxy groups regio- and stereoselectively.

raw_text: Our retrosynthetic analysis for the chemoenzymatic synthesis of alchivemycin A (1) is outlined in Fig. 2. Alchivemycin A (1) could be derived from the unnatural tetramic acid-bearing enzymatic substrate 8 by an enzymatic approach using the three oxidases AvmO1, AvmO2 and AvmO3. Compared with the natural substrate 3 (Fig. 1d), the unnatural substrate 8 has two more hydroxy groups at C-22 and C-24, which would be established via precise early-stage chemical synthesis rather than by using AvmO4 and AvmP, respectively. Notably, because compound 8 is similar to, but not exactly the same as the natural substrate, it may not be recognized by those enzymes. The highly functionalized intermediate 8 could be generated from compound 9 via aminolysis-induced macrolactamization and Lacey–Dieckmann condensation. Amine 9 could be derived by an $\mathsf { S } _ { \mathsf { N } } 2$ -type azidation of alcohol 10, which in turn could be constructed from the cis-decalin fragment 11 and the side-chain fragment 12 through a convergent boron-alkyl Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling reaction. The synthesis of the cis-decalin fragment 11 has been reported in the total synthesis of the vermisporin family of natural products<sup>6</sup>, while the side-chain fragment 12 should be readily prepared from the known compound 13 (ref. 8)

Convergent chemical synthesis of the unnatural enzymatic substrate

raw_text: The synthesis commenced with the construction of the integrated poly hydroxy side-chain fragment 12 starting from compound 13 (Fig. 3a). The hydroxy group in 13 was protected with a p-methoxybenzyl (PMB) group to afford compound 14 in 82% yield. Next, we regioselectively deprotected the terminal ketal group using 70% aqueous HOAc solu tion to furnish the diol 15 in 90% yield. The primary alcohol in 15 was selectively protected with an acetyl group to afford compound 16 in quantitative yield. After protecting the secondary alcohol with a tert-butyldimethylsilyl (TBS) group to obtain 17 in 88% yield, the acetyl group was deprotected using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL-H) to furnish 18 in 96% yield. Compound 18 was subjected to Dess–Martin periodinane (DMP) oxidation to yield the corresponding unstable aldehyde, which was directly treated with the alkenyllithium obtained from the reaction of alkene 19 with t-BuLi. The resulting crude product was deprotected with tetra-n-butylammonium fluoride (TBAF) to afford the diol 20 and epi-20 in a total yield of 71% over three steps (d.r. = 4:3). Based on the Cornforth–Evans transition state and polar Felkin–Anh model, the major product was identified as the desired product with the anti configuration<sup>37</sup>. The stereochemistry of the allylic alcohol in 20 was unambiguously confirmed by derivatization with 2,2-dimethoxypropane (2,2-DMP) and nuclear Overhauser effect (NOE) NMR spectroscopy (Fig. 3b). The diol 20 was then fully protected with methoxymethyl (MOM) groups. Finally, 1,2-dichloro-4 ,5-dicyanobenzoquinone (DDQ) was used to deprotect the PMB group to furnish the side-chain fragment 12 in 85% yield over two steps.

raw_text: cross-coupling reaction<sup>38</sup>. Thus, fragment 12 was first treated with 9-borabicyclo[3.3.1]nonane (9-BBN). After hydroboration, the excess 9-BBN was quenched with H O. The resulting boron-alkyl intermediate was used directly in the Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling reaction with the cis-decalin alkenyl iodide 11 to afford 10 in 99% yield. Next, we attempted to perform the azidation of the hydroxy group in 10 with an inversion of the configuration. We first screened the Mitsunobu reaction, using diphenylphosphoryl azide and diisopropyl azodicarboxylate as the reagents, but the desired azide product 22 could not be obtained. Azidation of the methylsulfonyl derivative of 10 by an S 2-type reaction was also unsuccessful. Fortunately, we were able to obtain the desired azide product 22 in 62% yield over two steps when the hydroxy group in 10 was activated with a trifluoromethylsulfonyl (Tf) group. Next, the silyl-protecting group in 22 was removed using TBAF and the corresponding primary alcohol was oxidized using DMP to give the aldehyde 23 in 85% yield over two steps. Aldol–DMP oxidation cascade reaction of 23 generated the β-keto ester 24 in 79% yield over two steps, setting the stage for the construction of the tetramic acid structure. We planned to use Staudinger reduction to convert the azide group into the amino group. Owing to their steric hindrance, bulky phosphines such as PPh failed to give the desired amino product. Thus, we used PMe to reduce the azide group in 24 and obtained the corresponding amino derivative 25 in 82% yield. Next, compound 25 was heated with methyl bromoacetate and K CO at mild temperatures to furnish the monosubstituted product 9 in 76% yield. The macrolactam 26 was then constructed in 94% yield by 4-dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP)-induced intramolecular aminolysis. With macrolactam 26 in hand, we first tried to establish the tetramic acid moiety by Lacey– Dieckmann condensation before deprotection. However, we failed to obtain the corresponding tetramic acid product due to the steric hindrance of the protecting groups (ketal and MOM) in 26. We then attempted to deprotect the ketal and MOM groups before carrying out the Lacey–Dieckmann condensation. Treating macrolactam 26 with concentrated HCl in MeOH resulted in deprotection and the crude product was used directly without further purification in the subsequent Lacey–Dieckmann condensation reaction with NaOMe as base to obtain the enzymatic substrate 8 in 69% yield over two steps. The UV absorption spectrum of 8 was similar to those reported for tetramic acids bearing acyl substituents $( \lambda _ { \mathrm { m a x } } = 2 9 2 \mathsf { n m } ) ^ { 3 9 , 4 0 }$ , indicating the presence of the 3-acyltetramic acid structure in 8.

Late-stage enzymatic synthesis

raw_text: After obtaining the enzymatic substrate 8, we focused on the end game using enzymatic reactions. We prepared AvmO1, AvmO2 and AvmO3 by heterologous expression in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) cells following the conditions reported by Ge and colleagues<sup>13</sup>. These three FAD-dependent oxidases were expressed with a His tag, purified using Ni nitrilotriacetate resin and desalted using a DP-10 column. With these three enzymes in hand, we first had to screen the enzymatic conditions for oxidation because compound 8 is not a natural substrate for these enzymes (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 2). Interestingly, we found that AvmO2 and AvmO3 could convert 8 into the corresponding monoepoxide products (27 and 28, respectively) very efficiently (>95% LC–MS yield), even though 8 is not the natural substrate for AvmO2 and AvmO3. However, when we treated 8 with AvmO1, the corresponding TDO ring product 29 was not observed by LC–MS. Treating 28 with AvmO2 led to the diepoxide product 30 (>95% LC–MS yield). However, we were unable to detect 30 when we treated 27 with AvmO3. Neither 27 nor 28 could be converted into the corresponding TDO ring products 31 and 32, respectively, by catalysis with AvmO1. We then treated the diepoxide 30 with AvmO1 and found that AvmO1 showed only weak activity towards the unnatural substrate 30 under the standard conditions (6% LC–MS yield). The low conversion of 30 stems from the fact that it is not a natural substrate for AvmO1, which has a narrow substrate scope<sup>13</sup>. Compared with the natural substrate 6 in the biosynthetic pathway (Fig. 1d), compound 30 has an additional hydroxy group at C-22, which would change the conformation of the macrocycle, hindering the recognition of the unnatural substrate 30 by AvmO1. We also tried to treat compound 8 with the three enzymes in a single pot, but not surprisingly, we detected only trace amounts of alchivemycin A (1) by LC–MS. Instead, the monoepoxide 27 (generated via catalysis with AvmO2) was observed as the only main product under these conditions. These results demonstrate that the sequence of the enzymatic reactions is crucial.

Late-stage enzymatic synthesis

raw_text: On the basis of the above results we began to optimize the enzymatic conditions for TDO ring formation in substrate 30 using AvmO1 (Supplementary Table 1). First, we increased the amount of enzyme to 20 mol%, which increased the LC–MS yield to 18%. Performing the reaction at 37 or 50 °C led to a drop in the yield. Next, we optimized the pH of the reaction. The use of citric acid–sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.0 or 4.0) resulted in the formation of a precipitate after the addition of the enzyme. We found that the best yield was obtained at pH 6.0. We also performed the reaction in 500 mM PBS at pH 6.0. To our delight, increasing the salt concentration improved the LC–MS yield to 30%. We also observed some precipitate formation in the reaction system after prolonged incubation, so we assumed that AvmO1 was unstable under these conditions. In a further attempt to increase the yield, we added AvmO1 in four portions every 4 h, which increased the LC–MS yield to 52%. Nevertheless, this approach required a high catalyst loading and the conversion remained moderate.

The residues important for protein stability and function probably remain the same throughout evolutionary history<sup>41</sup>. To improve the reaction outcome, we used a consensus site-searching strategy to engineer AvmO1 for consensus design, an approach that has previously been used to enhance protein stability and biological activity<sup>42,43</sup>. raw_text: AvmO1 as the query and subjected to consensus sequence analysis using the Consensus Finder web tool (http://kazlab.umn.edu)<sup>44</sup>. We conducted a brief survey of the 11 variants of AvmO1 with single-point substitution of sites with consensus site frequencies higher than 70% for Baeyer–Villiger oxidation activity under the optimized conditions for AvmO1. Of these, most variants displayed a higher conversion rate than AvmO1 (Fig. 5b). Surprisingly, introducing a single substitution, Y282R displayed 100% conversion under the optimized conditions. Consensus sequence analysis demonstrated that of the 827 homologous proteins of AvmO1, 97% have Arg at the corresponding position. To explain the mechanism of the improved activity, the structural model of AvmO1 with FAD was predicted using SWISS-MODEL (ref. 45), followed by 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations. Further alignment of the model with the reported crystal structure of the flavoprotein monooxygenase PgaE (Protein Data Bank ID: 2QA1)<sup>46</sup>, which shows high similarity to AvmO1 (42% sequence identity), elucidated that Tyr282 is close to these critical residues in the putative NADH binding groove (Supplementary Fig. 3). AvmO1, as a type O Baeyer–Villiger monooxygenase<sup>13</sup>, belongs to the class A flavoprotein monooxygenase (FPMO) subclass<sup>47</sup>. The enzymes in this subclass have conserved residues involved in NADPH binding<sup>48</sup>. Site-directed mutagenesis and kinetic, crystallographic and modelling studies have shown that p-hydroxybenzoate hydroxylase, a classic class A FPMO, binds with NADPH facilitated by the interactions of the side chains of Arg44, His162 and Arg269 with the pyrophosphate moiety of NADPH<sup>49</sup>. Late-stage enzymatic synthesis

raw_text: With the optimized variant AvmO1-Y282R in hand, we sought to establish a robust and efficient method to prepare alchivemycin A (1). To further reduce the catalyst loadings, the surfactant dl-α-tocopherol methoxypolyethylene glycol succinate (TPGS-750-M) was found to be an important additive. The use of this surfactant in water has been shown to notably increase the activities of some biocatalysts because the nanomicelles generated from the surfactant can house products that prevent the eventual saturation of the active pocket of the enzymes, that is, the so-called reservoir effect<sup>50–54</sup>. To our delight, with the addition of the surfactant TPGS-750-M, the unnatural substrate 8 could be fully converted into the corresponding monoepoxide 28 by catalysis with AvmO3 (1 mol%) in an isolated yield of 90%. Subsequently, under the same conditions, the monoepoxide 28 could be smoothly converted into the diepoxide 30 using AvmO2 (1 mol%) in an isolated yield of 95% (Fig. 5c). Compound 30 could also be obtained from compound 8 using the glucose dehydrogenase–NADP<sup>+</sup> recycling system<sup>55</sup>, in which only substoichiometric NADP<sup>+</sup> (0.15 equiv.) instead of superstoichiometric NADH (10 equiv.) needed to be added even though the catalyst loadings of AvmO2 and AvmO3 required 5 mol% (Supplementary Information). At this point, we focused on synthesizing the final natural product, alchivemycin A (1). raw_text: Conclusion
section_path: Chemoenzymatic total synthesis of alchivemycin A
Conclusion

raw_text: We have accomplished the total synthesis of alchivemycin A (1) using a chemoenzymatic approach that combines de novo skeleton construction and late-stage enzymatic oxidation reactions. The chemical synthesis of the unnatural enzymatic substrate features a boron-alkyl Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling reaction to connect the side-chain and cis-decalin fragments, the macrolactam structure was established by a robust intramolecular aminolysis and the tetramic acid ring was constructed by a Lacey–Dieckmann condensation reaction. The subsequent late-stage enzymatic epoxidations of the unnatural substrate with AvmO3 and AvmO2 furnished the corresponding epoxides regioand stereoselectively in high yields. Finally, the variant AvmO1-Y282R developed via rational protein engineering was used to establish the TDO ring system, leading to alchivemycin A (1). Notably, no currently available chemical methods could directly convert the tetramic acid ring into the TDO ring. The TDO ring is crucial for the biological activity of alchivemycin A (1) and represents a novel heterocyclic structure for medicinal chemistry. This work highlights the power of late-stage enzymatic oxidation for the efficient synthesis of complex natural products in a high state of oxidation. Although not optimal, these oxidative enzymes have already shown relatively good substrate scope. Further protein engineering would expand their catalytic efficiency and substrate scope to facilitate late-stage diversification of natural products and diversity-oriented synthesis of functionalized molecules<sup>56–65</sup>. This work also paves the way to develop a chemical probe based on alchivemycin A to study its antibacterial and anticancer mode of action and identify new cellular targets for drug discovery.

raw_text: Site-directed mutation of AvmO1
section_path: Chemoenzymatic total synthesis of alchivemycin A
Site-directed mutation of AvmO1

raw_text: The variants of AvmO1 were constructed by Megawhop PCR using the primers listed in the Supplementary Information. DNA fragments containing site-directed mutations were amplified with pET22b plasmid using wild-type AvmO1 or pQLinkHx plasmid with optimized AvmO1 as templates and AvmO1 forward primer with corresponding reverse primers as primers or AvmO1 reverse primer with corresponding forward primers as primers using FastPfu DNA polymerase (TransGen Biotech). The DNA fragments with the site-directed mutations were used as megaprimers and pET22b plasmid with wild-type AvmO1 as template for whole-plasmid PCR followed by DpnI (New England Biolabs) digestion at 37 °C for 5 h to obtain the vectors with mutations. The variants of AvmO1 were expressed and purified according to a previous report and stored at 4 °C for activity assays<sup>13</sup>.

raw_text: Synthesis of alchivemycin A (1)
section_path: Chemoenzymatic total synthesis of alchivemycin A
Synthesis of alchivemycin A (1)

raw_text: A solution of compound 30 (6.5 mg, 10.3 μmol) in dimethylsulfoxide (30 mM) was added to 250 mM PBS buffer (50 ml, pH 6.0) containing 1 wt% TPGS-750-M, followed by NADH (100 mM in H O, 1.0 ml) and AvmO1-Y282R (11.9 mg, 0.21 μmol, 2 mol%). After shaking at 20 °C (150 r.p.m.) for 24 h, the mixture was diluted with brine (50 ml) and extracted with EtOAc (3 × 80 ml). The combined organic layers were dried over anhydrous ${ \mathsf { N a } } _ { 2 } { \mathsf { S O } } _ { 4 }$ , filtered and concentrated in vacuum. The residue obtained was purified by preparative HPLC (MeCN–0.1% HCO H aqueous solution, from 40% to 100%), concentrated and freeze-dried to provide alchivemycin A (1) as a white solid (5.7 mg, 85%).
